Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has shown a partial radiologic response to intensive chemotherapy with disappearance of three lesions and ≥40 % shrinkage of the remaining disease. However, definitive determination of hepatic resectability requires critical information that is not provided: precise anatomic distribution of the residual lesions, volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant, baseline liver function, and status of the rectal primary (local stage, response to therapy, need for radiotherapy). Because these data are essential to decide whether a single‑stage or staged hepatic resection is feasible, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI or switch to a regimen incorporating targeted agents based on molecular profile) for 2–3 additional cycles to maximize tumor shrinkage and allow time for further imaging.  
- Obtain high‑resolution, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and 3‑D reconstruction to map all residual lesions, measure their size, and perform volumetric analysis of the future liver remnant.  
- Perform a thorough evaluation of the rectal primary: pelvic MRI and endorectal ultrasound to define T/N stage, assess mesorectal fascia involvement, and determine need for neoadjuvant chemoradiation.  
- If volumetry shows an insufficient FLR (<30 % in a normal liver, <40 % in a steatotic or chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
- Re‑stage the patient after imaging and functional assessment:  
   • If all residual lesions are confined to one hemi‑liver and an adequate FLR can be preserved, proceed to a single‑stage anatomical or non‑anatomical hepatic resection aiming for R0 margins.  
   • If lesions are bilobar and cannot be cleared safely in one operation, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant, PVE, then second stage resection) or a simultaneous resection of the primary rectal tumor with limited hepatic resection if oncologically appropriate.  
- Following hepatic surgery, complete adjuvant systemic therapy (total 12 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy) and consider postoperative radiotherapy to the pelvis if indicated by the rectal pathology.  
- Throughout, monitor CEA trends and repeat imaging every 8–12 weeks to detect early progression.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental location of residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
- Volumetric data: total liver volume and calculated future liver remnant.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Current staging and response of the rectal primary (MRI T/N stage, mesorectal fascia involvement, distance from anal verge).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted/immune therapy.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Details of prior or planned neoadjuvant radiotherapy for the rectal tumor.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
1. Completeness: Both recommendations address the major components of management for colorectal cancer with liver metastases, including resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative surveillance. They are aligned in covering these clinical domains, specifically discussing chemotherapy, liver MRI, volumetric analysis, and surgical resection strategies. Thus, they are substantially similar in this regard.

2. Step Concordance: Both recommendations agree on the resectability assessment, considering the case potentially resectable pending further information. In Step 2, both emphasize completing detailed imaging and planning before surgery, with a focus on potential surgical strategies. They both suggest systemic therapy continuation if resection is not immediately feasible. Therefore, they are aligned in their step-by-step approach.

3. Case-Tailoring Concordance: While both recommendations consider molecular profiling and liver lesion-specific factors, they differ in emphasis and detail. Recommendation 1 includes detailed information on the status of the rectal primary and specific lesion-related surgical options (PVE, ALPPS), while Recommendation 2 highlights parenchymal-sparing strategies and minimally invasive approaches, as well as liquid biopsy considerations. These differences indicate a lack of full alignment in tailoring to the specific case scenario.

4. Missing Data Concordance: Both recommendations identify similar critical missing information, such as precise lesion distribution, FLR, and rectal tumor status. Although there are differences in additional missing data (e.g., circulating tumor DNA in Recommendation 2), the core missing data are substantially aligned, focusing on imaging and liver-related metrics, making them concordant in this aspect.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- Rationale: After 4 cycles of systemic therapy the number of liver lesions has decreased from ten to three and all are <2 cm, indicating a good tumor response. However, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed because critical information is lacking:  
  • Precise anatomic distribution of the three lesions (unilobar vs bilobar) and their relationship to major hepatic vessels or biliary structures.  
  • Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve (e.g., ICG clearance, liver biochemistry).  
  • Status of the primary rectal tumor (resected, pending neoadjuvant chemoradiation, or still locally advanced).  
  • Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, PET‑CT, peritoneal assessment).  
These missing data are decisive for planning a curative hepatectomy; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the above assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy to deepen response and allow maximal tumor shrinkage:  
  • Maintain current regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) and add targeted agent appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease (anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody) if not already included.  
  • Administer 2–3 additional cycles, monitoring CEA trend and tolerability.  
- Restaging after the additional cycles:  
  • Multiphasic liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and volumetric analysis.  
  • Contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
  • Endoscopic evaluation of the rectal primary; if still locally advanced, proceed with neoadjuvant chemoradiation (long‑course 5‑FU based) followed by reassessment.  
- Surgical planning based on restaging results:  
  • If lesions are confined to a single hepatic lobe and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic liver), plan a single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (segmental or wedge resections) aiming for R0 margins.  
  • If lesions are bilobar with insufficient FLR, consider a two‑stage approach: first stage portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe to be resected, followed by reassessment of FLR and second‑stage hepatectomy.  
  • Simultaneous resection of the rectal primary (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) can be performed if the primary is resectable and patient’s performance status permits; otherwise schedule colorectal surgery after hepatic recovery.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: resume systemic chemotherapy (potentially with the same regimen) for 3–6 months, considering adjuvant anti‑EGFR therapy if indicated, and continue surveillance with serial CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact location of each hepatic lesion relative to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT).  
- Current status of the rectal primary tumor (size, T stage after chemotherapy, need for chemoradiation, surgical plan).  
- Results of chest imaging and/or PET‑CT to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Detailed chemotherapy regimen used (agents, doses, anti‑VEGF/anti‑EGFR inclusion) and tolerance.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations cover the major clinical management components: resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. Each includes detailed strategies for hepatic and rectal tumor management, systemic therapy continuation, and postoperative follow-up.

Step Concordance: Both recommendations follow the same reasoning regarding assessment of resectability and propose similar next steps: further imaging for detailed staging, consideration of systemic therapy to improve response, and planning based on resectability and FLR assessment. Both address the need to manage the hepatic and rectal components in a coordinated manner, even if specific details or techniques differ.

Case Tailoring: Recommendation 1 discusses RAS-wild-type and anti-EGFR therapy, whereas Recommendation 2 adds specific points on the differentiation grade and MSS/MSI status of the tumor, influencing prognosis and treatment. Recommendation 2 also mentions prehabilitation and ERAS protocols, which are not covered in Recommendation 1, indicating an additional layer of personalized care.

Missing Data Concordance: While both recommendations emphasize the need for data on lesion location, FLR, and primary tumor status, Recommendation 2 includes additional elements such as MSS/MSI mutation analysis and liquid biopsies, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. This shows a discrepancy in identifying critical missing data.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a single progressing hepatic lesion (5 cm in segment VII) after systemic chemotherapy, while the remaining lesions are stable or have disappeared. Surgical clearance would require control of the progressing lesion, either by down‑staging with additional systemic therapy or by local ablative treatment, before a definitive hepatectomy can be contemplated. The need for this prerequisite action (local control of the progressing metastasis) makes the case “Potentially resectable” rather than “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for at least 2–3 cycles to maintain disease control and assess further response.  
- Apply a local ablative modality to the progressing segment VII lesion: percutaneous radiofrequency/ microwave ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy, aiming for complete necrosis.  
- Re‑image (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) 4–6 weeks after local therapy to confirm response and to map the remaining stable lesions.  
- Perform volumetric liver assessment: calculate future liver remnant (FLR). If FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left liver.  
- Once adequate FLR is confirmed and all hepatic disease is controlled, plan a curative‑intent liver resection:  
   • If the stable lesions are confined to the left lobe, consider a left hepatectomy combined with wedge resections of any residual disease.  
   • If lesions are bilateral, consider a staged approach (right hepatectomy after PVE, followed by left‑sided resection) or a two‑step ALPPS procedure, depending on FLR and patient fitness.  
- Address the primary left‑colon tumor:  
   • If symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) – perform resection before or concurrently with liver surgery.  
   • If asymptomatic – consider simultaneous colon resection during the liver operation if operative time and physiologic reserve allow; otherwise, schedule colon resection after hepatic recovery.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy for at least 6 months, tailored to prior regimen and tolerability.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact anatomical distribution and size of the six stable hepatic lesions.  
- Relationship of lesions to major vascular structures (hepatic veins, portal pedicles).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Volumetric data to calculate future liver remnant.  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Details of prior chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles, and timing of last dose.  
- Serum tumor markers (CEA) trend.  
These data are essential to confirm resectability, select the optimal surgical plan, and finalize the multidisciplinary treatment sequence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
1. Completeness: The two recommendations differ significantly in terms of resectability assessment and management. Recommendation 1 considers the patient potentially resectable with a focus on achieving control over the segment VII lesion before proceeding with liver resection, including detailed surgical and systemic treatment plans. Recommendation 2 deems the case currently unresectable, emphasizing adaptation of systemic therapy and selective cytoreductive strategies rather than curative resection. The domains of surgical management and systemic therapy adaptation diverge significantly between the two.

2. Step Concordance: The key reasoning steps diverge; Recommendation 1 sees the case as potentially resectable, focusing on local control and curative resection plans following systemic therapy, whereas Recommendation 2 sees the disease as unresectable, focusing on systemic therapy adaptation and partial control via local treatments. Thus, they do not align in steps of resectability assessment or the management plan.

3. Case Tailoring Concordance: The recommendations focus on different aspects; Recommendation 1 is tailored towards achieving resectability with detailed strategies for local control and liver surgery, whereas Recommendation 2 is tailored towards systemic therapy adaptation and selective cytoreduction. Key case-specific elements such as systemic therapy adaptations and the extent of surgical intervention are handled differently.

4. Missing Data Concordance: Although both recommendations identify some common missing information (such as segmental distribution of lesions and FLR estimation), they diverge in other areas. Recommendation 2 uniquely requires molecular profiling and ctDNA analysis, which is not mentioned in Recommendation 1. There are also differences in emphasis, such as the need for surgical strategy details in Recommendation 1 versus systemic strategy details in Recommendation 2.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver metastases are radiologically absent after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but imaging alone cannot exclude microscopic residual disease. Definitive surgical planning requires confirmation that the original sites are still amenable to resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) and that the primary rectal tumor is resectable. Therefore a prerequisite step—high‑resolution liver MRI (with hepatocyte‑specific contrast) and possibly PET‑CT, plus assessment of liver function and FLR—must be completed before a definitive decision on liver surgery can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1. Restaging work‑up: obtain liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging, PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease, and calculate FLR using volumetric CT. Evaluate liver biochemistry, ICG clearance (if available), and performance status.  
- 2. Multidisciplinary review of restaging results:  
   • If imaging confirms no residual disease and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if liver steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated injury), proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery targeting the original metastatic zones (anatomic or non‑anatomic resection, or parenchymal‑sparing approach).  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the remnant, followed by resection once adequate volume is achieved.  
- 3. Primary rectal tumor management:  
   • If the primary lesion has responded and is resectable, schedule low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving surgery) either synchronously with liver resection (if operative risk acceptable) or in a staged fashion after hepatic surgery.  
   • If the primary remains locally advanced, consider neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery before or after hepatic resection, based on multidisciplinary consensus.  
- 4. Post‑operative systemic therapy: administer adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) after recovery, especially if high‑risk features (e.g., KRAS/NRAS mutation, poor differentiation) are present.  
- 5. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact location, size, and number of the original liver metastases (to determine resection extent and FLR).  
- Baseline and current liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance).  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Detailed staging of the primary rectal tumor (T stage, nodal involvement, distance from anal verge, response to any neoadjuvant therapy).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and surgical risk assessment.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) that may influence adjuvant therapy decisions.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Both recommendations cover the same major clinical domains, including resectability assessment, preoperative staging with imaging, surgical strategy, management of rectal primary, and postoperative systemic therapy and surveillance. Therefore, they are complete in terms of covering these key components.

In terms of step-by-step concordance, both recommendations identify the situation as potentially resectable with a need for precise restaging. The management plans proposed include similar sequences: imaging to assess liver and primary rectal tumor status, surgical considerations targeting the originally involved liver areas, and coordination with rectal surgery. 

However, in terms of case-tailoring, there are differences. Recommendation 1 discusses specific metrics for FLR and suggests distinct strategies (e.g., PVE or ALPPS) if FLR is insufficient, whereas Recommendation 2 includes a focus on local ablative techniques and mentions prehabilitation and ERAS protocols, which are not explicitly covered in Recommendation 1. Furthermore, Rec 2 emphasizes minimally invasive approaches for rectal surgery, which is not mentioned in Rec 1.

For missing data concordance, both recommendations identify the need for details on the initial liver metastases, liver function, rectal tumor status, and patient performance status. While Recommendation 2 adds liquid biopsy as a missing data point, the majority of critical missing information is in agreement between the two.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on imaging.  
- Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V leaves segments I‑III, VI, VII, VIII; resection of segment VII alone will preserve an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
- No vascular invasion described; lesion is anatomically approachable.  
- KRAS mutation does not affect technical resectability.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up  
  • Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and calculate ICG clearance if available.  
  • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to confirm FLR >30 % (or >40 % if underlying liver disease).  
  • Review prior systemic therapy exposure and performance status (ECOG 0‑1 preferred).  
- Surgical plan  
  • Proceed to an anatomic segmentectomy of VII (or non‑anatomic wedge if intra‑operative ultrasound confirms clear margins).  
  • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion borders and assess for additional occult disease.  
  • Aim for R0 resection with ≥1 cm margin when feasible.  
  • No need for portal vein embolization given expected adequate FLR.  
- Post‑operative oncologic management  
  • Pathology review for margin status, tumor regression grade, and molecular profile (KRAS confirmed).  
  • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (6 months) – preferred regimen FOLFOX ± bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease still benefits from anti‑VEGF).  
  • Consider enrollment in a clinical trial if available (e.g., adjuvant immunotherapy for microsatellite‑stable disease).  
- Surveillance  
  • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
  • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential data are lacking to make a reliable resectability assessment or to outline a definitive management plan. Essential information such as liver function, volumetry, performance status, and prior systemic therapy should be confirmed but is not currently a barrier to proceeding with the recommended approach.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment VII (3.9 cm) after a prior bisegmentectomy IV–V, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in a posterior segment and appears anatomically accessible while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior limited hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of segment VII.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and confirm preservation of portal inflow and hepatic venous outflow.

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the KRAS mutation and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered to address potential micrometastatic disease.

C. Close radiologic reassessment

Response:

Potentially resectable

- Initiate systemic therapy: 6‑8 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild‑type left‑sided primary.

   • Left hemicolectomy (either simultaneous or staged depending on patient condition).

- Post‑operative management includes continuation of adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 12 cycles, surveillance with serial CEA and imaging, and early assessment for any recurrence.

- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance) and volumetric FLR measurement.
